assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints as an amplification and propagation mechanism for credit cycles are a foundational building block of modern macro-finance. They underpin much of the post-2008 literature on financial frictions and macroprudential policy.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) are the clear originators of the collateral-based credit-cycle mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist are central to the related financial-accelerator and empirical strand, but that work builds on Bernanke-Gertler, and Bernanke's 2022 prize already recognised the financial-crisis and banking side. A two-person award is the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: The core papers are nearly three decades old and have been tested extensively, both theoretically and empirically, including in the 2007-09 crisis. Timing is fully mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises could count against it.
Whether the committee would add Gertler (and Bernanke's earlier work) to the attribution.
Citation influence is strong, but the empirical identification of the collateral channel is mixed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This body of work formalised how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes, and it created modern political economics as a field. It has wide influence across public finance, development and comparative politics.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the main authors of the constitutional and electoral-rule agenda. Besley's work on state capacity and political agency is closely linked and complementary. A three-person grouping is coherent, although the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity partly overlaps in subject matter.
assessment.maturity: The work spans more than 30 years, with a large empirical literature, including their own, confirming the main predictions. It is fully mature.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson) addresses related questions on institutions and may be seen as reducing the marginal case.
Some empirical results on electoral rules are sensitive to specification.
Other contributors to political economics, such as Alesina and Acemoglu, are not in the credited set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Mian and Sufi showed with granular data that household debt expansions drive credit booms, demand shortfalls and deep, prolonged recessions. This changed how macroeconomists and policymakers think about the 2008 crisis and about household balance sheets.
assessment.attribution: The two are the clear joint originators of the household-leverage and house-price/consumption evidence and its macro interpretation. Campbell's work on household finance and mortgage choice is related but distinct, so the pair is the sharper attribution.
assessment.maturity: The key work dates from about 2009 to 2015, with a book and a long follow-up literature. It is reasonably mature but younger than the top-ranked candidates, and the empirical-macro synthesis is still developing.
uncertainties: Some of the micro-to-macro aggregation claims remain debated.
The 2022 prize on banks and crises may overlap in the committee's view.
It is not yet clear how durable the 'credit supply versus demand' interpretation is.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the 'China shock' evidence reshaped understanding of labour-market polarisation, trade adjustment and the distributional effects of globalisation and automation. The work has strong policy and scientific impact.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the trade-shock papers. Hanson and Dorn are co-authors of the China-shock studies, and Katz is a major contributor to the skill-biased technical change literature. Task-model theory (Acemoglu-Autor, Acemoglu-Restrepo) is only partly captured, so the credit boundary is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The work is about 20 years old for the task framework and about 10 to 13 years old for the China shock. Long-term persistence results are still emerging, and some findings have been contested.
uncertainties: The credit boundary with Acemoglu, Restrepo and Katz is unclear.
The long-run interpretation of the China shock has been debated.
It overlaps with the 2021 recognition of empirical labour methods and with the 2024 prize on institutions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed international trade by explaining who exports, why trade raises productivity, and how gains from trade are distributed across firms. It is the basis of a large share of modern trade research.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the main originator, and Helpman provided the broader theoretical and empirical development with Melitz and Yeaple. Bernard, Jensen and Eaton-Kortum made closely related contributions that are not in this credited set, so attribution has a real boundary problem.
assessment.maturity: Over 20 years of theory and empirical testing have confirmed the main mechanisms. It is mature, though Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers the broader 'new trade theory' territory.
uncertainties: Credit boundary with Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum.
Partial overlap with the 2008 prize on trade and economic geography.
Redding is influential, but his work is later and more quantitative-spatial.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, the New Keynesian Phillips curve and the interest-rate-rule framework form the analytical core of modern monetary-policy analysis and central-bank practice. The importance is very high.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the weakest point. The work is spread across Calvo's staggered pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's integrative framework. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler made the empirical and estimated-DSGE contributions. A three-laureate cap forces a difficult selection, and earlier prizes (Phelps, Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims) overlap with parts of the territory.
assessment.maturity: The framework is decades old and embedded in practice, but its performance after the 2021-22 inflation episode is under reassessment.
uncertainties: Very high attribution ambiguity among many eligible contributors, and the choice of three names is contestable.
Post-2021 inflation has prompted criticism of the New Keynesian toolkit.
Overlap with previously honoured macroeconomists.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gave a quantifiable account of how distortions across firms explain a large share of cross-country income and TFP differences. It linked growth and development theory to micro data and spawned an extensive literature.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) are the central originators. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) made a closely related contribution, and Restuccia is credited here, but a two-person award is neater. Ownership of the idea is therefore split.
assessment.maturity: The core papers are about 15 to 17 years old and widely applied. Measurement of misallocation remains debated, so the empirical foundation is not yet settled.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of results to measurement error in firm-level data.
Credit shared with Restuccia and Rogerson.
The policy lessons are less direct than for other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The long-run top-income series and the wealth-distribution evidence transformed public and academic debate about inequality. The data-construction contribution is substantial, and the research agenda is influential across public economics, macro and history.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the foundational top-income series, with Zucman extending the work to wealth and offshore evasion. Zucman is a younger contributor, so a two-person recognition for the earlier series is easier to defend than three names. Atkinson, a major precursor, is deceased.
assessment.maturity: The income-series work is over 20 years old and has been replicated across countries. The theoretical interpretation, such as r>g, and the wealth-estimation methods remain contested.
uncertainties: Methodological criticism of the wealth and capitalisation estimates.
The theoretical claims have received less support than the data contribution.
Whether the committee would credit data construction and historical measurement at this level, and whether Zucman should be included.
